memory-injection.title: Process Injection Detection
memory-injection.description: Analyze a memory dump to identify suspicious processes. Look for code injection signs and malicious network connections.
memory-injection.q1: Which process shows signs of code injection?
memory-injection.q1_opt1: svchost.exe (PID 4284) — Suspicious DLL and C2 connection
memory-injection.q1_exp: svchost.exe (PID 4284) is suspicious because: 1) it loads a non-Microsoft DLL (msupdt.dll) from a temporary path, 2) it establishes an outbound connection to an external IP on port 443, 3) its parent process is not services.exe as expected.
memory-injection.q2: What injection technique is used here?
memory-injection.q2_exp: The attacker uses DLL injection (T1055): a malicious DLL (msupdt.dll) is loaded into the memory space of svchost.exe, a legitimate process, to hide.

disk-persistence.title: Persistence Mechanism Analysis
disk-persistence.description: Examine Windows disk artifacts to identify persistence mechanisms installed by an attacker.
disk-persistence.q1: Which artifact indicates persistence via Prefetch?
disk-persistence.q1_exp: The PowerShell Prefetch file with 47 executions in 2 hours is highly suspicious. Prefetch files show execution history and the abnormal frequency indicates automated activity, typical of a persistence script.

log-lateral-movement.title: Lateral Movement Detection
log-lateral-movement.description: Analyze Windows Event logs to detect lateral movement in the network. Identify the techniques used by the attacker.
log-lateral-movement.q1: Which Event ID indicates lateral movement via PsExec?
log-lateral-movement.q1_exp: Event ID 7045 (installation of a new service named 'PSEXESVC') is the most reliable indicator of PsExec usage for lateral movement. This service is temporarily created on the target machine.

timeline-attack.title: Attack Timeline Reconstruction
timeline-attack.description: Reconstruct the complete timeline of an attack from mixed events. Order events to understand the kill chain.
timeline-attack.q1: What is the first event in the attack chain?
timeline-attack.q1_exp: The attack chain begins with the phishing email (Initial Access - T1566) received at 09:14:22, followed by opening the malicious attachment which triggers code execution.

pcap-exfiltration.title: DNS Exfiltration Detection
pcap-exfiltration.description: Analyze network captures to detect data exfiltration via the DNS protocol. Identify suspicious queries.
pcap-exfiltration.q1: What DNS pattern indicates data exfiltration?
pcap-exfiltration.q1_opt1: TXT queries with long Base64-encoded subdomains
pcap-exfiltration.q1_opt2: Normal A queries to public DNS servers
pcap-exfiltration.q1_exp: DNS exfiltration typically uses TXT queries or very long Base64-encoded subdomains (e.g., aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.evil.com). The abnormal size of subdomains (>50 characters) is a reliable indicator.

browser-compromise.title: Browser Artifacts Investigation
browser-compromise.description: Examine browser artifacts from a compromised user. Reconstruct suspicious activity from history, cookies and downloads.
browser-compromise.q1: Which browser artifact reveals the initial infection vector?
browser-compromise.q1_opt1: History showing a visit to a drive-by download site
browser-compromise.q1_opt2: Cookie from a legitimate shopping site
browser-compromise.q1_opt3: Download of a PDF from a professional email
browser-compromise.q1_exp: The browsing history shows a visit to update-flash-player[.]com (malicious site mimicking Adobe) followed immediately by a download of 'FlashUpdate.exe'. This is a classic drive-by download.

registry-persistence.title: Registry Persistence Analysis
registry-persistence.description: Examine Windows registry keys to identify hidden persistence mechanisms. Analyze Run keys, Services and scheduled tasks.
registry-persistence.q1: Which registry key is used for persistence?
registry-persistence.q1_exp: The Run key under HKCU with a program named 'WindowsUpdate' pointing to C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\svchost.exe is a classic persistence mechanism. The name mimics a legitimate process and the Temp location is suspicious.
